title: At peace
hook: Asked if he had made his peace with God, Thoreau said he didn't know they had ever quarreled
tomorrow: where did Jesus say to worship: this mountain or that one?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Honi's carob tree: for after, fruit you may never taste. Today, the question families whisper about in hospital hallways.

Has she made her peace? Should someone call a chaplain? Should we even ask? Families have that conversation in hallways, and Henry David Thoreau's family had it too. As his friends told it, when Thoreau was dying, an aunt asked him whether he had made his peace with God. He answered that he didn't know they had ever quarreled. Another visitor tried to talk with him about the world to come. Thoreau's answer, as the story goes: one world at a time.
screen: `HAS SHE MADE HER PEACE?` → `THOREAU, DYING.` → `I DIDN'T KNOW WE'D QUARRELED.` → `ONE WORLD AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: No quarrel isn't a dodge, and it isn't a sermon. It fits the life he'd lived. He had once gone to live by Walden Pond, and in Walden he wrote why: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived." That's the Transcendentalist teaching Thoreau lived by: the sacred isn't something saved for the last hour. It's met now, in the pond, the woods, the day you're actually in. Live awake to this world, and there's no quarrel left to patch up at the end. One world at a time. Peace at the end can sound very different. Some people want a chaplain, a rabbi, a last prayer, and that peace is real too. What Thoreau shows is where his came from: it grew out of the days before. Which means it can start on any ordinary day, with one thing.
screen: `NOT A DODGE, NOT A SERMON.` · `I WISHED TO LIVE DELIBERATELY.` · `MET NOW, NOT SETTLED LATER.` · `PEACE GROWS FROM THE DAYS BEFORE.` · then, large: `NO QUARREL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small quarrel you've been carrying: with a person, a place, your body, your age. You don't have to settle it now. Breathe with it, and on a few out-breaths say softly, one world at a time, and let it be a little less of a fight.
At peace: for Thoreau, not a deal made at the end, but a life with no quarrel left to settle.
Your line: no quarrel. The peace at the end grew from the days before it. That's the week on aging and death, done.

howItsDone: Readers of Thoreau take his deathbed answers, no quarrel and one world at a time, as the fruit of a life lived deliberately, and look for peace in how they live ordinary days.

fork.setup: your mom keeps putting off the trips she loves: 'when I retire, I'll finally live.' what's Thoreau's answer?
options: live deliberately now; peace at the end grows out of days actually lived.
save the real living for later; that's what retirement is for, after all.

fork.reveal: Thoreau went to the woods so that, when he came to die, he wouldn't discover he had not lived. at the end, he had no quarrel left. no cabin required.

Thoreau.meaning: Henry David Thoreau, American writer of Walden, friend of Emerson

Walden.meaning: a pond in Concord where Thoreau lived; also his book

Transcendentalist.meaning: of Emerson and Thoreau's movement: the sacred met in nature and within

chaplain.meaning: a spiritual caregiver in a hospital, hospice or the military

sources.ref: Walden, ch. 2, 'Where I Lived, and What I Lived For'
